title: Real-world debugging scenarios
blurb: "It works locally but not in production." Scenario questions where the interviewer wants to hear your reasoning, not a memorised fact.

questions.q: Your API works locally but returns 401 in production immediately after deploy. What do you check first?
choices: Environment configuration — the signing key, issuer or audience differ between environments
Whether the frontend is on the right version
questions.why: A 401 means the token was rejected, not that the service is broken. Different secret, wrong issuer, or a clock skew making tokens look expired. 'What is different about that environment' is almost always the right first question.

questions.q: A page loads in 200ms locally and 8 seconds in production with the same code. Most likely cause?
choices: Data volume — a query that scans fine over 50 local rows scans 5 million in production
questions.why: Local databases are tiny and warm. Turn on query logging, run EXPLAIN on the slow one, and look for a sequential scan or an N+1. Seed a realistic amount of data locally and the problem shows up before release.
questions.asked: One of the best scenario questions there is — it separates guessers from people who instrument.

questions.q: Users report 'sometimes my changes don't save', but you cannot reproduce it. What is a likely explanation?
choices: A race — two requests, a lost update, or a client-side state overwrite after a slow response
The save button is too small
questions.why: Intermittent means timing. Look for a missing await, a fetch race, a lost update with no version check, or an optimistic update that never reconciled. Add a correlation id and log the write path.

questions.q: Memory grows steadily until the service is killed and restarted. Where do you look?
choices: Unbounded caches, listeners never removed, or accumulating references in a long-lived object
The size of the Docker image
questions.why: A cache with no eviction is the classic — it is a memory leak with a nice name. Take two heap snapshots under load and compare what grew.

questions.q: The frontend gets a CORS error calling your API. Where is the fix?
choices: On the server — it must send the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers and answer the OPTIONS preflight
In the browser, by disabling security
questions.why: Nothing the client does can grant itself permission. Check that OPTIONS is routed (not 404), that the origin is listed exactly, and that CORS middleware runs before anything that short-circuits.
questions.asked: The most common frontend/backend integration failure, and the wrong answer — 'mode: no-cors' — is very common.

questions.q: A request hangs forever instead of returning an error. What is the usual cause?
choices: A promise that never settles or rejects — a missing await, an unhandled rejection, or no timeout on an upstream call
The server is out of memory
questions.why: Every outbound call needs a timeout. Without one, one slow dependency ties up your connections until the whole service appears down — the failure spreads instead of being contained.

questions.q: You changed nothing and the build started failing. What is the most likely reason?
choices: A dependency resolved to a new version because the range was not pinned or the lockfile was not used
questions.why: 'Nothing changed' usually means nothing *you* changed. Check whether CI runs `npm ci`, whether a base Docker image tag moved, or whether a GitHub Action was pinned to a floating tag.

questions.q: A React list shows the wrong data in the wrong rows after deleting an item. What is it?
choices: Index used as key, so component state stayed attached to positions rather than items
The API returned the wrong order
questions.why: Classic. React matched by position, so row 3's local state (an open editor, a checkbox) now belongs to a different item. Use a stable id.

questions.q: An endpoint is slow only for one large customer. What do you suspect?
choices: An unbounded query with no pagination, or a missing index on the tenant column
questions.why: Behaviour that scales with one tenant's data volume points at the data access. Multi-tenant systems need the tenant column in the index and hard limits on result size.

questions.q: Logs show the error but not which user or request it belongs to. What is missing?
choices: A correlation id attached to every log line for a request, propagated to downstream calls
questions.why: Without it you cannot reconstruct one request's path through concurrent traffic. Generate an id at the edge, put it in the logging context, and return it in error responses so a user report maps to a log query.
questions.asked: The strong answer mentions propagating it to downstream services.

questions.q: A deploy succeeded but users see a blank page with a console error about a missing chunk. What happened?
choices: Their browser holds the old HTML referencing hashed bundles the new deploy removed
questions.why: A classic SPA deploy failure. Fixes: keep old assets around for a grace period, cache the HTML shell short and the hashed assets long, and handle a chunk load error by reloading the page.

questions.q: A background job runs three times per night instead of once. Why?
choices: Three instances are running and each has its own scheduler — it needs a distributed lock or a single scheduler
questions.why: An in-process scheduler scales with your replicas. Either elect a leader, take a distributed lock, or move scheduling to infrastructure that runs it once.

questions.q: The same data appears twice after a user double-clicked Submit. What prevents it properly?
choices: Server-side idempotency — a unique constraint or an idempotency key — not just a disabled button
questions.why: The UI fix helps, but a retry, a flaky connection or a direct API call bypasses it. Only the server can guarantee 'this happens once'.

questions.q: Dates are one day off for some users. What is the cause?
choices: Timezone handling — a UTC timestamp rendered in local time, or a date-only value treated as midnight UTC
The database is in the wrong region
questions.why: `new Date('2026-03-01')` is parsed as UTC midnight, which is the previous day west of Greenwich. Store instants in UTC and calendar dates as plain dates — they are genuinely different types.

questions.q: You get a 502 from your API behind a load balancer. What does that usually mean?
choices: The upstream app did not respond acceptably — it crashed, is not listening, or exceeded the proxy timeout
The client sent a bad request
questions.why: Check the app's own logs and health endpoint first — the proxy is reporting a symptom. Common causes: the container crashed on startup, it bound to localhost instead of 0.0.0.0, or a request exceeded the proxy's timeout.

questions.q: How do you approach a bug you cannot reproduce?
choices: Narrow the conditions with logs and data, form a hypothesis, and add instrumentation to confirm or kill it
Add try/catch until it stops erroring
questions.why: The method matters more than the answer: what is different about the failing cases — user, tenant, browser, time, data shape? Bisect the difference rather than guessing at fixes.
questions.asked: An open question where the interviewer is listening for a systematic process.

questions.q: A test suite passes but the same code fails in production. What is the most useful reflection?
choices: The tests did not cover the boundary — real data, real config, real concurrency, or a real dependency
questions.why: Heavily mocked tests verify your assumptions, not reality. When a bug escapes, the useful question is 'what kind of test would have caught this?' — and often the answer is an integration test.

questions.q: Your service degrades under load: response times climb until requests time out. First hypothesis?
choices: A bounded resource is exhausted — connection pool, thread pool, or an upstream limit — and requests are queueing
questions.why: Latency climbing while throughput plateaus is a queueing signature. Find what is saturated: pool metrics, upstream latency, GC pauses. Adding instances without fixing the bottleneck often makes it worse by adding more contention.

questions.q: A user says 'the site is broken' with no other detail. What do you ask for?
choices: What they did, what they expected, what happened, when, and any id or error text on screen
Their password so you can reproduce it
Whether they tried a different browser
For them to file a formal ticket
questions.why: Reproduction steps and a timestamp let you find the request in the logs. This is also why a user-visible correlation id on error pages is worth the small effort.

questions.q: You find the cause of an outage. What comes after the fix?
choices: A blameless write-up: what happened, why, and what change stops the whole class of problem recurring
questions.why: The valuable output is the systemic change — a test, a guardrail, an alert, a process — not the individual patch. Interviewers ask about this to see whether you think past the immediate fire.
questions.asked: A maturity question. 'Blameless' is the word worth using.

questions.q: The browser shows stale data after an update, but the API returns the new value in curl. Why?
choices: A caching layer is serving the old response — browser cache, service worker, CDN, or client-side query cache
The user needs to log out
questions.why: Work outward from the client: devtools with cache disabled, then check Cache-Control headers, the CDN, and whether the frontend cache was invalidated after the mutation.

questions.q: What is the first thing to do when production is broken?
choices: Restore service — roll back or mitigate — then investigate the cause
Find the root cause before touching anything
questions.why: Recovery and diagnosis are separate goals. Rolling back to a known-good version stops the damage and buys you time to investigate properly — which is why fast, safe rollback is worth engineering for.
